title: Nematic Wigner crystals in rhombohedral multilayer graphene
authors: Yang Ge, Ashwini Malviya, Ethan Angerhofer, Zhengguang Lu, Jiabin Yu
abstract: Recent experiments have reported evidence for Wigner crystals (WCs) in rhombohedral graphene. Here, we investigate Wigner crystallization in rhombohedral tetralayer graphene using projected Hartree-Fock (HF) calculations and time-dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) calculations. We first perform HF calculations with one electron per Wigner unit cell, and find nematic WCs (nWCs) that spontaneously break the threefold rotational symmetry $C_3$ and $C_3$-invariant WCs. In particular, there are two nWC regions in the phase diagram: one larger region at large displacement fields and low electron densities, and another smaller region at intermediate fields and high densities. Both the nWCs and the $C_3$-invariant WCs are valley-polarized states with zero Chern number, and have positive indirect gaps in the HF band structure. We then perform TDHF calculations to further test the local stability of the WC states. We find that all $C_3$-invariant WCs and half of the nWCs are locally stable, while the remaining nWCs are unstable towards WCs with two electrons per unit cell or metallic states. The predicted stable nWC phase can be identified experimentally by scanning tunneling microscopy through its anisotropic charge distribution or by angle-resolved transport measurements via a direction-dependent depinning voltage.
summary: The authors investigate Wigner crystallization in rhombohedral multilayer graphene, focusing on the emergence of nematic crystal states that spontaneously break rotational symmetry. Using HF and TDHF calculations, they map out the phase diagram, predicting stable nWC phases favored by kinetic energy effects over $C_3$-invariant states. The predicted stability boundaries can be experimentally verified using STM or transport measurements.
main_problem: The study investigates Wigner crystallization (WC) in rhombohedral multilayer graphene, specifically determining if nematic phases (nWC) spontaneously break the threefold rotational symmetry ($C_3$) compared to standard $C_3$-invariant WC states.
main_result: Hartree-Fock calculations predict stable nWC regions favored over $C_3$-invariant WCs in certain parameter regimes due to kinetic energy gains, while TDHF analysis confirms stability for only half of the predicted nWC phases.
method: The research employs projected Hartree-Fock (HF) and Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) calculations on a continuum model Hamiltonian. Stability is rigorously tested by analyzing the eigenvalues of the RPA stability matrix derived from TDHF.
model_or_system: The system is rhombohedral tetralayer graphene ($	ext{R4G}$) modeled using a projected many-body Hamiltonian incorporating spin and valley degrees of freedom. Electron repulsion is treated via a screened Coulomb interaction.
key_observables: Nematicity diagnostic ($N$), stability eigenvalues from TDHF, anisotropic charge distribution (for STM), and direction-dependent depinning voltage (for transport measurements).
important_parameters: Electron density ($n_e$) ranging from $0.2$ to $0.4 	imes 10^{12} 	ext{ cm}^{-2}$, and displacement fields ($V_{	ext{disp}}$) between $40$ and $100 	ext{ meV}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the projected HF framework, assuming a fixed two-body interaction; TDHF only proves local quadratic instability.
figures_summary: Figure 1 maps the HF phase diagram showing regions of $C_3$-symmetry violation (nWC) and instability. Figure 10 shows the smallest TDHF stability eigenvalue across the parameter space, distinguishing instabilities towards unit cell doubling (blue labels) versus metallic/stripe phases (red labels).
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first using HF calculations to identify symmetry-breaking nWC states in specific phase diagram regions. It then uses TDHF theory to test the local stability of these candidate WC states, identifying which ones are stable and predicting experimental signatures for their detection.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for understanding correlated electron phases (Wigner crystals) in 2D materials like graphene, using advanced many-body techniques (HF/TDHF) to predict symmetry breaking and stability boundaries.

(a),(c) Band structures and (b),(d) real-space charge den- sities for the representative C3-invariant WC [the circle in Fig. 1(a), displayed in (a) and (b) here], and nWC [the star in Fig. 1(a), displayed in (c) and (d) here], respectively. The rugged dispersion in (c) arises from imperfect commensuration between the discretized continuum k mesh and the Wigner Bloch momentum points.

FIG. 3. Lowest eigenvalue branch of the TDHF stability matrix for (a) a C3-invariant WC [the circle in Fig. 1(a)] and (b) an nWC [the star in Fig. 1(a)]. The first Wigner Brillouin zones (BZs) are outlined in white. In both cases, the eigenvalues are positive at q ̸= 0 and zero (within numerical error) at q = 0, indicating local stability of the HF solution.

FIG. 4. Momentum-space origin of the nWC at ne = 0.25 × 1012 cm−2 and Vdisp = 90 meV. (a) Noninteracting Fermi sea of a spin-valley- polarized state, showing the three-lobed low-density Fermi surface (in black) produced by trigonal warping. (b) Occupation n(k) of the nWC ground state. (c) Occupation n(k) of the lowest-energy C3-invariant WC solution at the same parameters. This higher-energy solution preserves the threefold occupation pattern and spreads weight over the three lobes.

The k-path is part of the Γ–K–M trace that extends from K by 9.55% of the distance towards Γ, and by 20.1% of the distance towards M.
